1:
Chrysostom opens by distinguishing two deaths. The bodily one carries no crime and no peril, being a matter of nature rather than of deliberate choice, taking its origin in the transgression of the first man and passing thence into a nature, and in any case shortly brought to an end; the spiritual one, being a matter of choice, has criminality and has no termination. He adds a remark on the writer's manner, that having said they had arrived at the very last degree of wickedness he takes care not to distress them excessively, since men are put to shame when their former misdeeds are brought forward even after those deeds are cancelled. Henry divides the state into two, that sinners are dead in state, destitute of the principles and powers of spiritual life and cut off from God who is the fountain of it, and dead in law, as a condemned malefactor is called a dead man. Clarke takes the legal sense as primary, that having sinned they were condemned and might be considered dead in law, incapable of any legal act and liable at any moment to a punishment already deserved. Calvin insists it is no danger of death but a real and present one.

Whether the two nouns differ is answered three ways. Ellicott holds they are brought together to form a climax, the first signifying a swerving aside and falling and the second an entire missing of the mark, so that even in the plural the second denotes positive principles of evil doing while the first points to failure in particular acts by men not necessarily out of the right way. Wesley divides them by nation instead, taking sins to be spoken chiefly of the Gentiles who knew not God and trespasses of the Jews who had the law and yet disregarded it. Robertson notes only that both stand where the later verse has one. Henry declines the distinction, taking the pair for all sorts of sin, habitual and actual, of heart and of life. Calvin adds that the metaphor of death was used by classical writers too, though not of spiritual death, of which they knew nothing, but of the absence of moral principle, and he quotes Epictetus telling his hearers that the instructor is dead and they are dead. Clarke reports the same broad usage, that death is employed by all writers and in all nations to express extreme misery.

The phrase about the prince of the power of the air is called unique and difficult by Ellicott, who resolves it in two steps: it signifies not a power over the air but a power dwelling in the region of the air, and the word for power is used almost technically in this epistle of superhuman power, so that the Evil One is ruler of such power considered collectively. Robertson supplies the physics behind the word, that the ancients used it of the lower and denser atmosphere against another term for the higher and rarer, and remarks that those who deny a personal devil cannot successfully deny the crime waves of modern men. Wesley describes the power as unspeakably penetrating and widely diffused while holding it beneath the orb of believers as to its baneful influence. Ellicott and Robertson both note the two words rendered world, one meaning the appointed period and the other the material and sensuous character of things, so that the former life is described as at once transitory and carnal; Clarke and Wesley take the first word rather of a long succession of corrupt ages, and Calvin denies that it means the course God ordained or the elements, taking it for the depravity that pervades the whole world.
4:
The word rich draws comment from nearly everyone, and two of them fill it out with the sense it carries elsewhere. Barnes calls it a beautiful expression and turns it on the reader's own values: men are often rich in gold and silver and pride themselves on it, but mercy is the wealth of God, and he is so rich in it that he can make all blessed. Calvin's editor collects the classical parallels, that the best writers use rich and riches in this metaphorical way, one speaking of the riches of philosophy and the Roman orator of the riches of the mind, meaning the excellencies of understanding and virtue. Ellicott observes that the idea of richness in grace, glory and mercy is especially frequent in this epistle and lists the places. Gill distinguishes the mercy that is general and providential toward all men from the special mercy exhibited only in Christ, and explains the epithet by the freedom and liberality of the dispensing, the number of the recipients and the variety of the channels, in covenant, mission, redemption, regeneration, pardon and salvation, while remaining inexhaustible.

Love and mercy are distinguished rather than merged. Henry separates them by their object, love being God's inclination to do us good considered simply as creatures and mercy regarding us as apostate and miserable, so that the eternal good-will is the fountain from which every mercy proceeds. Clarke orders them the same way, making infinite love the groundwork which in reference to us assumes the form of mercy, and mercy in turn provides the Saviour. Barnes presses what the love was shown toward, that it was love to the children of wrath, love to those who had no love to return, and remarks that a man loves his friend and his benefactor while God loves his foes and seeks to do them good. On the timing of the clause about being dead, Barnes and Ellicott disagree. Barnes construes it with the loving, holding that God did not quicken us while we were dead but loved us then and made provision; Ellicott says the words should be connected not with loved us but with quickened, since he brought life out of spiritual death. Robertson notes only that the pronoun shifts here from you Gentiles to us.

That the raising and the sitting are spoken of as done already is the difficulty of the passage, and it is met by an appeal to union. Calvin grants that these blessings are not yet seen by mortal eyes and that as respects ourselves salvation is still the object of hope, but holds that in Christ we already possess a blessed immortality, since what has hitherto appeared only in the head belongs truly to the members by the secret union; of everything we now want we have a sure pledge and foretaste in his person. Barnes reasons the same way from the closeness of the connection, that the resurrection of the head made that of the members certain, as raising the whole body together, and that the entrance of our representative into heaven is the pledge of ours. Wesley marks the tense plainly, calling it spoken by way of anticipation, since believers are not yet possessed of their seats though each has a place prepared. Gill allows the raising to be read either of the spiritual resurrection or of the bodily one, called already accomplished because it is certain and because the people rose in Christ as their representative. Barnes adds the purpose: that the conversion of such sinners should stand as a perpetual encouragement to others.
8:
What the pronoun in and that not of yourselves refers to is argued on grammatical grounds, and the grammar is agreed. Barnes states it plainly: the pronoun is neuter while the word for faith is feminine, so it points not to faith but to the salvation by grace just described, which he calls the obvious interpretation and now generally conceded. Clarke sets out the Greek and reaches the same verdict, that the neuter cannot stand for the feminine noun but has the whole preceding sentence for its antecedent. Robertson adds that the word for grace is feminine too, so the pronoun refers to neither but to the act of being saved by grace on the condition of faith. Wesley agrees that it covers the whole clause. What is curious is that the witnesses disagree about who dissents: Barnes names Doddridge, Beza, Piscator and Chrysostom among those who refer the pronoun to faith, while the note printed with Calvin cites Chrysostom, with Theodoret and Theophylact, for exactly the contrary reading, quoting Theophylact that he does not say faith is the gift of God but that to be saved by faith is the gift. Barnes calls the point theologically small in any case.

Calvin sets the two halves against each other as a division of labour. On God's side salvation is unmixed grace, since he declares he owes us nothing and it is no reward or recompense; on man's side the question is only how the offered thing is received, and the answer is by faith, which strips us of all commendation and brings a man empty to God that he may be filled. From that he draws the polemical conclusion, that we ought to be silent about free will, good intentions, fancied preparations, merits and satisfactions, each of which claims a share of the praise; and he compresses the argument of two whole epistles into three phrases, that righteousness comes from the mercy of God alone, is offered in Christ by the gospel, and is received by faith without the merit of works. Ellicott makes a finer distinction between the two formulas commonly treated as identical, holding that justification by faith names one completed act while salvation by grace names a continuous state lasting till the judgment, and that the latter suits this epistle better because its whole idea is the continuous indwelling in Christ. He notes the wording answers almost verbally to Peter's at the council in Jerusalem.

The word rendered workmanship is taken by Robertson from the verb for making with an ending denoting result, and used here not of the original creation but of the moral and spiritual renewal; Ellicott notes it occurs elsewhere only of God's works in creation and thinks the first creation not excluded, since we are his wholly and absolutely, though the next clause shows the new creation is meant. On the phrase about good works Ellicott offers an unusual rendering, on the basis or condition of good works, the works being future in themselves yet contemplated as already existent in God's foreknowledge and inseparable from the regenerate life; and he calls the following clause perhaps the strongest expression in all scripture of the mystery of predestination, since it covers not merely the call and regeneration but the very works in which free will is most plainly exercised. Calvin turns this against his opponents phrase by phrase: the apostle does not say we are assisted, nor that the will is prepared and then left to run by its own strength, nor that the power of choosing rightly is bestowed and the choice left to us, but that we are God's work. Clarke and Wesley both hold the line from the other side, that we are not saved for good works but saved in order to perform them.
11:
The command to remember is treated as having a purpose, and the purpose is disputed only in emphasis. Chrysostom explains why it was needed at all, that when men are raised from great meanness to corresponding or greater dignity it is usual with one and all not so much as to retain any recollection of their former condition, being nourished in the new glory. Barnes turns it into a recommendation of the faculty itself, that no power of the mind can be better employed to produce humility, penitence, gratitude and love than the memory, and that it is well to recall former sins and dwell on our hardness of heart until the heart is affected. Gill gives three ends together, to magnify the grace of God in their conversion, to humble them by a view of their former state, and to teach them that they could never be saved by works of their own; Clarke adds that they may ever see and feel their obligation to live a pure life. Chrysostom notices the rhetorical management as well, that the writer lowers the advantages of the one party and admires the disadvantages of the other, arguing with each according to their character.

On the two party names Ellicott hears contempt in the verb. That both sides are said to be called by their titles implies the names were now mere names and virtually nothing, and he collects the other forms the same denial takes elsewhere, circumcision set against obedience to God's commandments, against faith working by love, against the new creation, and against the unity of all in Christ. He then finds in the added phrase about hands a contrast between a carnal circumcision belonging to the unbelieving and a spiritual one belonging to Christians. Robertson observes that the abstract nouns are used to describe the two peoples, and that the word for made by hands is a verbal adjective agreeing with the second. Henry reads the taunt sociologically, that hypocritical professors value themselves chiefly on external privileges and reproach those destitute of them. Calvin takes the missing sign more gravely than the others, since circumcision was the token distinguishing God's people and its absence the mark of a profane person, and since God usually connects his grace with the sacraments the want of them is taken as evidence that his grace was wanting too — though he adds at once that the argument does not hold universally.

Ellicott reads the catalogue of losses as one root and two branches. The condition is summed up first in being separate from Christ, and from that are drawn two consequences: that they had no part in the covenant, being alienated from the commonwealth and strangers to the covenants of the promise, and that being left in the world they had no hope and were godless in thought and act — since Christ is at once the substance of Israel's covenant and the revealer of God, so that to be without him is to lose both covenant and light. He presses one word, that the text says not aliens but alienated, implying that the covenant was the true birthright of humanity from which mankind had fallen. Calvin argues the same dependence from the promise, that all the promises hang on the one made to Abraham and lose their value without it, so that to take away the covenant of salvation is to leave no hope. Robertson notes the word for commonwealth occurs only twice in the New Testament and that the term for godless means both being without God and hostility to him. Clarke and Barnes both explain far off and near from Jewish usage about access to the temple.
14:
Robertson insists on the pronoun: it is he himself who is our peace, not merely what he did, necessary as that was. Ellicott makes the same point by comparison, that whereas the Old Testament promises a prince of peace and the Lord elsewhere gives peace, here alone he is called not the giver but the peace itself, his own nature being the actual tie of unity between God and mankind and between man and man. Ellicott also warns that a double meaning runs through the whole passage, peace between Jew and Gentile and peace between both and God, and that it is not always easy to tell which branch a given expression belongs to; he suggests comparing the parallel in Colossians, where only the second branch appears. Calvin turns the title into an assurance and a rebuke at once: let no one who dwells in Christ doubt that he is reconciled to God, and let the Jews who despised that grace while boasting themselves the holy people observe that if Christ is the peace then all who are outside him are at variance with God. Barnes draws the practical rule, that the best way to end alienation between minds is to bring them to the same Saviour.

The middle wall is identified with the temple barrier by most and with something looser by one. Robertson gives the archaeology, that a partition in the temple courts divided the court of the Gentiles from the court of Israel with an inscription forbidding a Gentile to go further, and recalls the uproar when the apostle was accused of taking a Greek past it; he adds that the compound noun is very rare anywhere, known from one papyrus and one inscription. Henry makes the wall the ceremonial law itself, so called by allusion to that same partition. Clarke doubts the allusion is so precise, taking the expression of the whole distinction that Jewish laws and customs made, and reporting the alternative that it refers to their ancient practice of living apart with a river or a wall between themselves and their heathen neighbours; he adds that wherever they went their own rites were a sufficient separation. Calvin illustrates the abolished marks by a contemporary parallel, that circumcision, sacrifices, washings and forbidden foods distinguished Israel as the white and the red cross distinguish the French of his own day from the Burgundians, and that a prince uniting two contending nations would remove the badges of their former enmity.

The grammar of the next clause is admitted to be unsettled. Ellicott reports that the enmity may stand in apposition to the wall of partition or to the law of commandments, while holding the general sense little affected either way; Robertson thinks it doubtful that the enmity is the object of the verb for abolishing at all, preferring to read it in apposition to the wall, so that the enmity between Jew and Gentile simply was the partition, and he weighs likewise whether in his flesh belongs to the breaking down or to the abolishing, allowing sense in both and preferring the first. Ellicott presses the verb itself, which elsewhere means to supersede by something better, and draws the consequence that the law is abolished as a law in ordinances, that is in the letter, and established in the spirit. Barnes reads the same phrase as a doctrinal marker, observing that nobody would say of a moral teacher that he accomplished a result by his flesh, so that the words are such as only a man who believed in a sacrifice would use. Calvin gives the mechanism plainly, that the Son of God by assuming a nature common to all formed in his own body a perfect unity.
19:
Paul stacks two words for the outsider, and Barnes separates them: xenoi are foreigners in a state as opposed to citizens, while paroikoi are guests in a private family as opposed to its members, a distinction he credits to Rosenmuller. He then fills in what such standing meant at Athens. A resident stranger could live and trade undisturbed but had no voice in the public deliberations and no part in the management of the state; he could not transact business in his own name, and had to choose a citizen as patron to guard him against injustice, which Barnes documents from Potter's Greek Antiquities. Ellicott makes the same pair alien and half-alien, and adds that the sojourner's nearer position sharpened rather than softened the exclusion, since daily contact with citizens pressed the sense of being shut out from power and privilege. Clarke reads the whole chapter as a city holding rights by charter, where an uncircumcised God-fearer might dwell in the land as one who rents but never owns. Ellicott then notices that the two replacements answer the two exclusions term for term: fellow-citizens answers to stranger, household answers to foreigner, because the unit in ancient law is always the family and not the individual.

Verse 20 divides the readers over whose foundation is meant. Ellicott holds it impossible to take the prophets here as those of the Old Testament: the order of the two nouns, the comparison with two later passages in this same epistle, and the stress on present against past that runs through the chapter appear to him decisive. Barnes takes them as the older prophets and so reads the phrase for revealed doctrine at large, given through prophet or apostle alike; Gill and Clarke agree, Clarke naming it the doctrine taught by the prophets in the Old Testament and the apostles in the New. Ellicott next canvasses three senses of the foundation of the apostles and prophets, dismissing as forced both the foundation on which they rest and the foundation they laid, and adopting with most ancient authorities the reading that makes the men themselves the foundation, since Paul here calls Christ not the foundation but the corner-stone which, in a remark Ellicott draws from Chrysostom, binds walls and foundations together. Calvin resists: the word means doctrine, no patriarchs or kings are named but only appointed teachers, and strictly Christ alone supports the whole. Both he and Barnes notice how loudly Peter goes unmentioned.

The last two verses turn a finished building into a growing one. Robertson presses the missing article: without it, ordinary Greek idiom asks for each several building rather than all the building, though he grants it is not perfectly clear what that means, and he thinks Paul coined the participle for fitly framed together, an architectural word found only here and at one later place in the epistle. Ellicott defends the familiar rendering while allowing every act of building as the alternative, and observes that Paul, finding the corner-stone relation too slight to carry the church's union with Christ, soon leaves it for the body and its head. Calvin orders the two verbs: first the fitting-together, believers accommodating themselves to one another, for otherwise there is no building but a confused mass, and the chief part of that symmetry is unity of faith; increase only follows. Clarke refuses the popular guess that Paul glances at the temple of Diana, insisting the Jerusalem temple is in view, since that alone was a house where God dwelt between the cherubim; Barnes says simply that God once filled the temple and now fills the church and the hearts of his people. Gill sees beams, rafters and pillars proportioned for the strength of the whole.
